html:
Pip: There is a genre of week that ends with you standing in the sun, wallet empty, on hold, being offered a personal loan. Sakti has lived it, written it, and somehow made it into something worth thinking about.

Mara: This episode follows a single piece by Sakti that moves from a failed ATM transaction to a surprisingly elegant cable installation — and lands on a question about what education and institutional life do to the empathy we started with.

Pip: Let's get into it.

We Were Born Intelligent. Education Ruined Us.

Mara: The post opens with two encounters that seem unrelated — a power cut that swallowed ten thousand rupees, and an electrician who redesigned a cabling job without being asked. The tension between them is the whole argument.

Pip: The ATM scene sets the stakes fast. The money leaves the account, doesn't arrive in the hand, and then — while Sakti is standing in a dark, dirty room watching a machine reboot with what the post calls "more dignity than urgency" — the bank's call centre agent pivots to a credit card offer.

Mara: That moment gets named directly. The post says: "She was not unkind. She was transactional. And that, I think, is the sadder thing."

Pip: Transactional is the sharper word, because it removes blame and replaces it with something structural. She wasn't cruel. She was following a script that had no field for "customer is standing in the sun, empty-handed."

Mara: And the post is careful to say the system did eventually work — the money came back a week later. The failure isn't that the process broke. It's that nobody in the process paused to feel the gap.

Pip: Which is where the electrician walks in and quietly dismantles the argument that empathy is a professional skill you acquire in workshops.

Mara: He had a tenth-standard education. No certification in design thinking. What he did was listen, pull in the society electrician, walk the flat, and come back with a plan the post describes as "neater, more complete, and frankly more elegant than anything I had pictured when I made the call."

Pip: The post's conclusion isn't that institutions are evil. It's quieter and more uncomfortable than that — "We were born intelligent. We were born empathetic." Something closes off that capacity somewhere between childhood and the quarterly targets.

Mara: The line that lands the diagnosis is this: "We have made ourselves transactional. We do our job to get the salary to reach our account. And because we have become a transaction to our employers, we begin to treat others as transactions too."

Pip: So the circle closes. Not through malice. Through accumulated habit.

Mara: And the post ends not with a call to learn more, but to remember — the electrician didn't know the terminology for what he was doing. He just did it, because, as the post puts it, "nobody had yet taught him not to."

Pip: That's the uncomfortable part. The training isn't what gave him the skill. The training is what the rest of us received instead.

Mara: The real question underneath all of it is what gets optimized out of people when institutions measure outputs instead of understanding.

Pip: And whether the work is addition or recovery. More to come.
